summary: Defines a framework for coupling the Active Queue Management algorithms of two queues, for flows that respond to congestion differently. It offers a path for the Internet to move from classic Reno-friendly congestion control to scalable congestion control with very low queuing delay. It is an experimental specification.

plainLanguage.summary:
L4S is about delay. The idea is that a router keeps two queues at its bottleneck: one for ordinary TCP-style traffic and one for newer traffic that reacts to congestion much faster. The router then links the two so that neither group gets more of the link than the other.

The point is that the fast-reacting traffic gets a very short, very steady wait in the queue while the ordinary traffic keeps the throughput it had before.

questions: how do l4s and classic traffic share a bottleneck
what is the coupling factor k in l4s
why does l4s use two queues
subtitle: Two linked queues let low-latency Scalable traffic and Classic TCP-style traffic share one link fairly without per-flow inspection.

tldr.problem: Classic TCP-style congestion control needs a large queue to keep a link full, so queuing delay stays high and varies. Newer Scalable congestion controls can keep a link full with almost no queue, but on their own they would push Classic traffic out of the way.
tldr.mechanism: The router keeps two queues, one for each kind of traffic, and links them. The Classic queue's marking probability is tied to the square of the L4S queue's, so both kinds of flow get roughly the same throughput while the L4S queue stays nearly empty.
tldr.outcome: The RFC fixes the framework and its requirements rather than one algorithm, and gives two example algorithms in its appendices. It is an Experimental document, and it needs the matching ECN protocol in RFC 9331 to work.

today: RFC 9332 is an Experimental document and has not been obsoleted. It is the network half of the L4S work: RFC 9330 describes the overall architecture and RFC 9331 the ECN protocol that end systems use with it.

sections.title: The Problem With Classic Congestion Control
sections.content:
Latency is becoming the critical performance factor for many applications on the public Internet, among them interactive web, voice, conversational video, online gaming and remote desktop. Once access network bitrates reach the levels now common in the developed world, further increases give diminishing returns unless latency is addressed too. Queuing remains a major intermittent component of latency.

Very low latency has so far only been available to a few selected low-rate applications that confine their sending rate within a specially carved-off portion of capacity, which is prioritised over other traffic, for example Diffserv Expedited Forwarding. It has not been possible to let any number of low-latency, high-throughput applications seek to fully use available capacity, because the capacity-seeking process itself causes too much queuing delay.

Recent active queue management in the network, such as Flow Queue CoDel, PIE and ARED, has reduced queuing delay for all traffic. But however good the AQM is, the capacity-seeking rate of TCP-like congestion controls sets a floor: the queue either varies or the link sits underused. These AQMs are tuned to let a typical Reno-friendly flow produce an average queue that roughly doubles the base round-trip time, which adds 5 to 15 ms of queuing on average, and a 99th percentile queuing delay of 20 to 30 ms. Research into congestion control in the end system alone, such as BBR, seems to have hit a similar floor of about 20 ms on average.

L4S learns from Data Center TCP, which shows that two small but radical changes to congestion control cut the two main causes of queuing delay variability: far smaller rate variations than Reno-friendly controls, and a shift of smoothing from the network to the sender. Both changes only work together with a complementary change in the network, and both are only feasible with ECN rather than drop, because without ECN the resulting high marking levels would become very high loss levels.
sections.plainLanguage: Ordinary TCP keeps a link busy by pushing back on itself, and the queue that builds up while it does so is what makes the connection slow. The newer methods react quickly enough to keep the queue almost empty, but only if the network cooperates.

sections.title: Classic and Scalable Traffic
sections.content:
The DualQ Coupled AQM uses two queues for two services. The Classic service is intended for all the congestion control behaviours that coexist with Reno, such as Reno itself, CUBIC and TFRC, and the Classic queue is a queue providing that service. The L4S service is intended for traffic from Scalable congestion control algorithms such as Prague, and the L4S queue is a queue providing that service. The L4S service is for more general traffic than just Prague, so that the set of congestion controls with similar scaling properties can evolve.

A Classic Congestion Control is a behaviour that can coexist with standard Reno without significantly harming its flow rate. Because flow rates have scaled since TCP congestion control was first designed in 1988, it now takes hundreds of round trips, and growing, to recover after a congestion signal, whether a loss or an ECN mark. Control of queuing and utilisation therefore becomes very slack, and the slightest disturbance, such as new flows starting, prevents a high rate from being attained.

A Scalable Congestion Control is one where the average time from one congestion signal to the next, the recovery time, stays invariant as the flow rate scales. DCTCP, for example, averages 2 congestion signals per round trip whatever the flow rate. Scalable controls keep the same degree of control over queuing and utilisation at any flow rate, and high throughput stays robust to disturbances.

For L4S the four names of the 2-bit IP ECN field are unchanged from the original ECN specification: Not-ECT, ECT(0), ECT(1) and CE, where ECT stands for ECN-Capable Transport and CE for Congestion Experienced. A packet marked with CE is called ECN-marked.
sections.plainLanguage: Classic traffic is everything that behaves like ordinary TCP. Scalable traffic is the newer kind that reacts in step with the round trip, so its queue never has to build up to keep the link busy.

sections.title: The Coupled AQM
sections.content:
The design starts from the 1990s TCP formula, which relates the steady-state congestion window of standard Reno to the drop probability p. To a first-order approximation, the steady-state window of Reno is inversely proportional to the square root of p. The design focuses on Reno as the worst case, because if it does no harm to Reno it will not harm CUBIC or any traffic designed to be friendly to Reno.

DCTCP behaves differently: its congestion window is inversely proportional to the marking probability, not to its square root. Scalable is used for all congestion control behaviours that behave this way.

For safe coexistence a Scalable flow has to run at roughly the same rate as a Reno TCP flow, all other factors being equal, so the drop probability for Classic traffic, p_C, has to be distinct from the marking probability for L4S traffic, p_L. The original ECN specification required these to be the same, but RFC 8311 updates it to allow them to differ.

The Coupled AQM makes the Classic drop probability proportional to the square of the coupled L4S probability p_CL, which is an input to the instantaneous L4S marking probability p_L but changes as slowly as p_C. The squaring of p_CL counterbalances the square root of p_C in the TCP formula, so the Reno flow rate ends up roughly equal to the DCTCP flow rate. The relation is:

p_C = ( p_CL / k )^2

where k is the constant of proportionality, called the coupling factor. The L4S ECN protocol says that k does not have to be standardised for interoperability, but that a value of 2 is recommended. The choice of k is a matter of operator policy. It does not affect relative flow rates when all flows are Classic or all are L4S, and it does not affect the relative throughput of small flows.
sections.plainLanguage: The link between the queues is a single number, k, and the RFC suggests 2. The bigger it is, the more the Classic traffic is penalised relative to L4S traffic.

sections.title: The Dual Queue Structure
sections.content:
A classifier separates incoming traffic between the two queues, L and C. Each queue has its own AQM that decides the likelihood of marking or dropping, p_L and p_C. The AQM for Classic traffic works in two stages: a base stage that outputs an internal probability p-prime, and a squaring stage that outputs p_C. Substituting into the coupling equation gives p' = p_CL / k, so the slow-moving input to ECN marking in the L queue is p_CL = k*p'.

The L queue uses a Native AQM that calculates a probability p-prime-L as a function of the instantaneous L queue delay. Because the L queue has conditional priority over the C queue, whenever the L queue grows the AQM ought to apply that probability, but p_L ought not to fall below p_CL. This gives p_L = max(p'_L, p_CL), which has also been found to work well in practice.

After the AQMs have applied their dropping or marking, a scheduler forwards their packets to the link. The scheduler gives priority to the L queue, but not as strongly as the coupling from the C queue, because as the C queue grows the base AQM applies more congestion signals to L traffic, and the L flows then use less of the scheduling share. Because the scheduler is work preserving it schedules any C traffic in the gaps. Priority has to be conditional to prevent the C queue from being starved in the short term, which also gives short Classic messages such as DNS requests better response times.

Classification uses the ECN field rather than flow identifiers: the ECT(1) and CE codepoints identify L4S packets. This means the coupling can achieve coexistence without inspecting transport-layer flow identifiers, which is not always practical or desirable. An operator may still steer particular packets into the L queue, but a network node must not change Not-ECT or ECT(0) into an L4S identifier, so the L queue is more generally a low-latency queue. Two example algorithms are given in the appendices: DualPI2, which uses a Proportional Integral controller as the base AQM, and Curvy RED, derived from RED with delay-based configuration parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: Traffic goes into one of two queues based on the two-bit ECN field in the packet header, so the router never has to look at which flow a packet belongs to. The L queue is served first, but the C queue is not locked out, and the two queues feed each other's congestion signals.

sections.title: What an Implementation Must Do
sections.content:
The normative requirements are written so that they hold for any AQM designed for a single queue that generates a statistical or deterministic mark or drop probability driven by the queue dynamics.

An implementation must comply with the prerequisite L4S behaviours for any L4S network node, must use two queues each with an AQM algorithm, and the AQM for the L queue must be able to apply ECN marking to ECN-capable packets. The scheduler draining the two queues must give L4S packets priority over Classic, although the priority must be bounded so that Classic traffic is not starved, and it should be work-conserving or close to it, so that Classic traffic can fill any space left by L4S traffic. The AQM must apply ECN marking to traffic in the L queue that is no lower than that derived from the likelihood of drop or ECN marking in the Classic queue using the coupling equation.

When a packet that does not carry the expected ECN codepoint is classified into a queue, the requirements are weaker, because operator-specific classifiers exist for flexibility. An ECT(0) packet in the L queue should get CE marking with a probability appropriate to Classic congestion control. A Not-ECT packet in the L queue should be forwarded unchanged if separate queue protection is provided, and should be dropped with a Classic-like probability if it is not. An ECT(1) packet in the C queue should get CE marking using the coupled probability p_CL. If the DualQ has detected overload it must introduce Classic drop to both types of ECN-capable traffic until the overload episode has subsided.

By default a DualQ Coupled AQM should not need any configuration for use at a bottleneck on the public Internet. Optional settings include extra classifiers, the expected typical and maximum round-trip time, the coupling factor k, a limit on the conditional priority of L4S, and the maximum Classic ECN-marking probability before drop is introduced. An implementation should also let the operator monitor, per queue and per sample interval, the bits forwarded, the packet counts for arrived, presented to the AQM and forwarded, the ECN packets marked and the packets dropped, and the queue delay, with mean and 99th percentile queue delay derivable per queue per sample interval.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC sets out what any implementation has to do, so that different vendors' routers can be told apart by behaviour rather than by algorithm. It also says what the router should report so that an operator can see what is happening in each queue.

sections.title: Unresponsive Flows and Overload
sections.content:
The privacy argument for the DualQ approach is that users who encrypt application flow identifiers, for example in IPsec or other encrypted VPN tunnels, do not have to sacrifice low delay. On the question of policing, the RFC explains that users' interests do not collide in the same way for delay as they do for bandwidth: getting more bandwidth on a shared link necessarily means someone gets less, whereas queuing delay can be reduced for everyone. Per-flow rate policing is therefore separable from a basic AQM, as an option under policy control, and the DualQ gives low delay without prejudging that question.

Handling unresponsive flows matters, because in the absence of any per-flow control the basic DualQ must give unresponsive flows no more throughput advantage than a single-queue AQM would. The goal is that the DualQ behaves no worse than a single-queue AQM when the total load of unresponsive flows is within the link capacity. Tests showed this is the case with no mechanism beyond the regular coupled DualQ. Whether the unresponsive flow classifies itself into the L or the C queue, the system behaves as if it has subtracted from the overall link capacity, and the coupling shares out the remaining capacity between the competing responsive flows.

Overload is handled by requiring drop for both types of ECN-capable traffic until the episode subsides, and by making the priority of the L queue conditional so that the C queue is not starved in the short term. The RFC is explicit that the choice of how much each class should give up under overload, in throughput, delay or drop, is for the developer or for operator policy rather than for the IETF.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the router never looks at which flow a packet belongs to, it also cannot police one flow against another, and the RFC treats that as a separate, optional choice. If the link is overloaded, both kinds of traffic have to give up something, and the RFC leaves the choice to the operator.

viz.caption: The parts of a DualQ Coupled AQM

items.title: IP-ECN classifier
items.text: Splits incoming traffic between the L and C queues using the ECT(1) and CE codepoints.

items.title: L4S queue and Native AQM
items.text: Holds Scalable traffic. Its AQM computes a marking probability from the instantaneous queue delay.

items.title: ECN marker
items.text: Marks packets in the L queue with the CE codepoint instead of dropping them.

items.title: Classic queue and Base AQM
items.text: Holds Classic traffic. Its AQM outputs an internal probability that is then squared.

items.title: Drop or mark
items.text: Drops or marks packets in the C queue, using the squared probability.

items.title: Conditional priority scheduler
items.text: Serves the L queue first, but bounds that priority so Classic traffic is not starved.

viz.caption: The probability relations that define the coupling

data.title: Coupling equations
data.code:
p_C  = ( p_CL / k )^2
p'   = p_CL / k
p_CL = k*p'
p_L  = max(p'_L, p_CL)
